lines: Last topic ended with a small log file holding a deferred change, merged in only when someone reads. That log file deserves its own close look.
Today's question is what's actually inside it, and today it gets built for real, bit by bit, and checked against three real table formats at once.
Picture a data file whose rows mostly need to stay exactly as they are, except for a small slice that has to be marked gone, without rewriting a single byte of the file.
What's the leanest possible way to record which rows those are?
answer: There's no single leanest answer in the abstract — it depends entirely on how many rows you're marking.
A plain list and a bitmap trade places as the cheaper option, and the crossover point is exactly what's worth building next.

lines: Here's the actual shape it takes. Picture every row in the file laid out in order, and a single bit sitting beside each one.
A bit flipped on means its row is gone. Nothing about the file itself ever changes — only this separate strip of bits does.
This wasn't just described — it was actually built. A small slice of rows, well under a real fixed threshold the format itself defines, got marked this way for real.
And under that threshold, the honest, cheapest structure turned out to be nothing more than a short, plain list of exactly which positions were marked.
Now push on that same idea harder. Keep marking more and more rows gone, climbing well past wherever that threshold sits.
Does the list just keep stretching forever, one more entry for every additional row, or does something about its shape actually change?
answer: Something changes, and deliberately so. Past that threshold, a growing list stops being the cheap option at all.
The structure switches to one fixed-size strip of bits instead — one that costs exactly the same no matter how many more rows get added.

lines: Also built for real, and past that same threshold this time: the structure really did flip over into one fixed-size strip of bits.
And that's the whole point of the switch — past a certain density, a bitmap beats a list every single time, by never growing another byte larger.
Here's the catch nobody should skip past. Marking a row gone this way costs almost nothing to write — but it was never actually free.
Every single time anyone reads that file afterward, they now have to check this extra strip of bits against every row, just to know what's still really there.
And that extra checking was measured directly, not assumed — reading the file while honoring those marks really did take noticeably longer than reading it with nothing marked at all.
The fix is a deliberate housekeeping pass that finally rewrites the file for real, dropping every marked row for good — and once that ran, reading sped right back up.

Here's something worth sitting with. Two of the three major table formats agreed on building this exact same bit-strip trick — not just a similar idea, but literally the same underlying format, on purpose, for compatibility.
The third format never adopted that trick at all. It solves the identical problem by writing a note straight into its own small side file instead — no bit strip in sight.
So here's the whole shape of it. A strip of bits beside a file buys you a delete that costs nothing to write.
But that bargain was never free — every read pays a little of it back, right up until a deliberate rewrite clears the debt for good.
